meta.title: Who really said “I was born for soccer, just as Beethoven was born for music”? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Pelé did compare himself to Beethoven — but the documented wording is longer and comes from a 2012 FIFA.com interview. The short ‘soccer’ form is unsourced.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said ‘I was born for soccer, just as Beethoven was born for music’?
meta.ogDescription: The wording Pelé is documented saying is longer, and from a 2012 FIFA.com interview. The short ‘born for soccer’ form traces only to an unreadable book.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1940–2022 · Brazilian footballer, three-time World Cup winner
answer.sourceLine: Pelé really did make this comparison, and made it on the record — but not in these words. The only citation anyone offers for the short “born for soccer” wording is Wikiquote’s pointer to Parton Keese’s sports book The Measure of Greatness, whose text is not readable online. The wording Pelé is documented saying is longer and names a painter too, from a FIFA.com interview syndicated 21–22 February 2012.

source.heading: Where the wording comes from

docMeta.dd: Parton Keese, The Measure of Greatness
Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs, N.J.; catalogued 1981, cited by Wikiquote as 1980. Scan is lending-restricted — text not checkable.
FIFA.com exclusive interview, syndicated 21–22 February 2012 — longer, and names Michelangelo as well as Beethoven.
Not recorded — neither reprint states whether the interview was conducted in Portuguese or in English.

source.excerpt: My father used to say to me: ‘You were born to play football. You’ve got a gift for it. But if you don’t work at it and you don’t practice, then you’ll be just like the rest.’ He was absolutely right, but then again, I was born to play football, just like Beethoven was born to write music and Michelangelo was born to paint.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ carries the exact short wording in its main sourced Quotes section, with a single citation beneath it: Parton Keese, The measure of greatness (1980).

The book is real. The Internet Archive catalogue record ↗ lists it as Parton Keese, The Measure of Greatness (Englewood Cliffs, N.J.: Prentice-Hall), ISBN 0135678005, 190 pages, catalogued 1981 — but the scan is access-restricted, so its text could not be searched.

The readable attestation is a FIFA.com interview, reprinted by the Oceania Football Confederation on 21 February 2012 ↗ and by ASEAN Football on 22 February 2012 ↗, in which Pelé says football, not soccer, and names Michelangelo too.
Quote Investigator ↗ has never written this one up — a site search returns nothing — so there is no specialist ruling to defer to here.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording Pelé is documented saying, from the FIFA.com interview reprinted on 21 February 2012 — not the shorter “born for soccer” form that circulates online.

source.rightsNote: Both candidate sources are modern: the FIFA.com interview was published in February 2012, and Keese’s The Measure of Greatness was issued by Prentice-Hall around 1980–81. Either way the wording is far too recent to be public domain in the United States, so it is treated as in copyright to Pelé’s estate and the publisher of whichever text it first appeared in.

author.name: Pelé
author.heading: Who was Pelé?
author.metaLine: 1940–2022 · Brazilian footballer · three-time World Cup winner
author.bio: Edson Arantes do Nascimento — Pelé — was born in Três Corações, Minas Gerais, on 23 October 1940 and died in São Paulo on 29 December 2022. He spent almost his entire career at Santos, from 1956 to 1974, before a late American chapter with the New York Cosmos from 1975 to 1977, and he remains the only footballer to have won three World Cups: 1958, 1962 and 1970. Much of his career was recorded in Portuguese, which is why many a famous “Pelé quote” in English is really a translator’s or a reporter’s rendering rather than a transcript.

The wording Pelé is documented saying is longer: “I was born to play football, just like Beethoven was born to write music and Michelangelo was born to paint,” FIFA.com interview, syndicated 21–22 February 2012.

misattribution.heading: Right man, wrong words
misattribution.intro: No one else claims this line. The problem is not the speaker — it is the wording, and the fact that the citation everyone repeats has never been opened.

items.why: Quote sites print it as though it were the original. Every one of them traces back to the same single note on Wikiquote ↗, which cites Parton Keese’s The Measure of Greatness. That book exists, but its Internet Archive scan ↗ is access-restricted, so the page cannot be read and the wording cannot be confirmed.

On the record Pelé named a painter as well as a composer: “I was born to play football, just like Beethoven was born to write music and Michelangelo was born to paint,” per the FIFA.com interview reprinted 21 February 2012 ↗. The popular short form drops half the comparison.

In the interview the line answers something Pelé’s father told him about practice, quoted just before it in the ASEAN Football reprint ↗. Cut loose, it reads as boasting; in place, it is a point about talent needing work.

Pelé was Brazilian, and nothing on the record settles the language question: neither reprint of the FIFA.com interview says whether it was conducted in Portuguese or in English. Where a Pelé line reaches English through a translator or a reporter — as many of his most-quoted lines did — the choice between “soccer” and “football” is that person’s, not his.
Pelé attracts free-floating inspirational lines. Even Wikiquote’s own page ↗ carries items such as “Success is not an accident…” with no citation attached at all.

misattribution.truthLine: Pelé did make the comparison, and he made it publicly — to FIFA.com, in an interview reprinted 21 February 2012 ↗, in a longer form that also names Michelangelo. The trimmed “born for soccer” wording is a retelling nobody has yet tied to a readable source.

context.heading: Why the short version travels further
lead: Pelé is one of the most quoted athletes who ever lived, and many of his most-quoted English lines are renderings rather than transcripts — he was Brazilian, and much of his life on the record was in Portuguese. Renderings drift. The tell here is the word “soccer.” The version Pelé is documented giving FIFA in February 2012 says football, and it names two artists, not one: “I was born to play football, just like Beethoven was born to write music and Michelangelo was born to paint.”

The shorter, tidier “born for soccer, just as Beethoven was born for music” is the form quote sites reprint, and every one of them stops at the same citation — Wikiquote’s note pointing to a 1980s American sports book that no one can currently open. That is not evidence of fabrication. It is evidence that nobody has checked.
context.detailsSummary: What Pelé actually said in the 2012 interview
detailsBody: In the FIFA.com interview, the comparison arrives as an answer to something his father told him. Pelé quotes him first — “You were born to play football. You’ve got a gift for it. But if you don’t work at it and you don’t practice, then you’ll be just like the rest” — and then agrees, adding the Beethoven and Michelangelo line. Stripped of that setup, the sentence reads as pure self-regard. In context it is the opposite: a point about talent being worthless without work.
When AFP compiled its Pelé quote roundup on 29 December 2022, it used the FIFA.com wording, not the “soccer” one.
context.pull: The tell is the word “soccer.” On the record, Pelé said football — and he named Michelangelo too.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Pelé page lists "I was born for soccer, just as Beethoven was born for music" in its main sourced Quotes section, citing Parton Keese, The measure of greatness (1980); the same page also carries "Success is not an accident..." with no citation.
The Internet Archive catalogues Parton Keese, The measure of greatness (Englewood Cliffs, N.J.: Prentice-Hall), ISBN 0135678005, 190 pages, year 1981, as an access-restricted lending item.
An article dated 21 February 2012, sourced to FIFA.com, quotes Pelé: "I was born to play football, just like Beethoven was born to write music and Michelangelo was born to paint."

An ASEAN Football article dated 22 February 2012, sourced to FIFA.com, carries the fuller passage in which Pelé quotes his father ("You were born to play football...") before the Beethoven and Michelangelo comparison.
AFP's 29 December 2022 quote roundup attributes "I was born to play football, just like Beethoven was born to write music and Michelangelo was born to paint" to "Pele to Fifa.com".
Wikipedia gives Pelé as Edson Arantes do Nascimento, 23 October 1940 - 29 December 2022, Santos 1956-1974 and New York Cosmos 1975-1977, with World Cup wins in 1958, 1962 and 1970.
A Quote Investigator site search for "born for soccer" returns no results, confirming QI has no article on this quotation.
LibQuotes reproduces "I was born for soccer, just as Beethoven was born for music" with the citation "quoted in Parton Keese, The Measure of Greatness (1980)".
